# Submit SQL Query > Submit SQL Query

Use the `POST /api/v3/query` endpoint of the Data 360 Query API to execute a SQL query against your Data 360 data. Submit a query in ASYNC mode to receive a `queryId` for polling, or use ADAPTIVE mode to receive results immediately when the query completes quickly. Both modes support JSON and Apache Arrow response formats.

:::important
This API is the recommended interface for new integrations. See [Migrate from Query API V1 and V2](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/data-cloud-query-api-reference/query-api-migration.md) for guidance on updating existing code.
:::

metadata.breadcrumb: Submit SQL Query > Submit SQL Query

document:
# Submit SQL Query > Syntax

- **HTTP Method**: POST
- **Format**: REST
- **URI**: `/api/v3/query`

# Submit SQL Query > Request Headers

| Header          | Value                                                                 |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Authorization` | `Bearer {accessToken}`                                                |
| `Content-Type`  | `application/json`                                                    |
| `Accept`        | `application/json` (default) or `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` |

# Submit SQL Query > Request Body (Part 1)

| Field           | Type    | Required | Description                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| --------------- | ------- | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `sql`           | string  | Yes      | SQL query to execute. Uses Data 360 SQL syntax.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `transferMode`  | string  | No       | Execution mode. Accepted values: `ASYNC`, `ADAPTIVE` (default).                                                                                                                                           |
| `paramStyle`    | string  | No       | Parameter binding style. Accepted values: `QUESTION_MARK` (default), `NAMED`, `DOLLAR_NUMBERED`. See [Parameterized Queries](#parameterized-queries).                                                     |
| `parameters`    | array   | No       | Array of parameter objects for parameterized queries. Each object requires `type` (a Data 360 SQL type name) and `value` (a JSON string). See [Parameterized Queries](#parameterized-queries).            |
| `settings`      | object  | No       | See [Query Settings](#query-settings) for supported keys.                                                                                                                                                 |
| `resultRange`   | object  | No       | Controls what is returned within the REST response. ADAPTIVE mode only. Supported keys: `rowLimit` (integer), `byteLimit` (integer, default and maximum 20 MB).                                           |
| `queryRowLimit` | integer | No       | Maximum number of rows to produce by the query. Acts as an implicit `LIMIT` clause. The query won't produce more rows than this value. Set to `0` to retrieve only the schema without producing any rows. |

# Submit SQL Query > Query Settings

The `settings` object accepts the following keys:

- `timezone` — Time zone identifier for date and time values, for example `"Etc/UTC"`.
- `language` — Language identifier for locale-specific formatting, for example `"de_DE"`.
- `date_style` — Order of year, month, and day for parsing date strings. Accepted values: `MDY`, `DMY`, `YMD`. See [Date/Time Input](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/datetime.md#date-time-input).
- `lc_time` — Locale for date literals, as an ISO language and country code, for example `"en_US"` or `"de_AT"`.
- `query_timeout` — Execution limit in milliseconds before the query is terminated, for example `1800000` (30 minutes).

# Submit SQL Query > Parameterized Queries

The `paramStyle` request field controls how parameters are bound in your SQL:

- `QUESTION_MARK` (default) — Use `?` placeholders
- `NAMED` — Use named placeholders (`:paramName`)
- `DOLLAR_NUMBERED` — Use positional placeholders (`$1`, `$2`, ...)

Each object in the `parameters` array requires a `type` and a `value`.

- `type` — A [Data 360 SQL type](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/datatypes.md) name, such as `varchar`, `bigint`, or `boolean`. For types that take a length or precision, include the relevant field, for example `{ "type": "varchar", "length": 10, "value": "abc" }`.
- `value` — The parameter value, always passed as a JSON string. Even for numeric types, pass the value as a string, for example `"42"`, not `42`.

:::note
`type` takes SQL type names, not JSON type names. Use `varchar` rather than `string`.
:::

# Submit SQL Query > Response Structure

Both ASYNC and ADAPTIVE modes share a common response structure.

# Submit SQL Query > Response Headers

Both ASYNC and ADAPTIVE modes return these response headers.

| Header             | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Date`             | Timestamp when the response was generated.                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `Content-Type`     | `application/json` or `application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` depending on the `Accept` request header.                                                                                                                                 |
| `x-hyperdb-status` | JSON-serialized string containing the full query status. Fields: `queryId`, `completionStatus`, `chunkCount`, `rowCount`, `progress`, `expirationTime`, and `executionStats`. Use the `queryId` from this header to poll for results. |

# Submit SQL Query > Response Body — ASYNC Mode

In ASYNC mode, the response body omits the `data` field and `returnedRows` is `0`. Use the `queryId` from the `x-hyperdb-status` response header to poll `GET /api/v3/query/{queryId}` for completion.

| Field          | Description                     |
| -------------- | ------------------------------- |
| `metadata`     | Object containing column schema |
| `data`         | Omitted in ASYNC mode           |
| `returnedRows` | Always `0` in ASYNC mode        |

metadata.breadcrumb: Submit SQL Query > Response Body — ASYNC Mode

document:
# Submit SQL Query > Response Body — ADAPTIVE Mode

If the query completes within the adaptive timeout, `data` contains the result rows. If the query exceeds the adaptive timeout without producing rows, the response mimics ASYNC mode: the `data` field is omitted and `returnedRows` is `0`. Use the `queryId` from the `x-hyperdb-status` response header to poll `GET /api/v3/query/{queryId}` for completion.

| Field          | Description                                                                      |
| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `metadata`     | Object containing column schema                                                  |
| `data`         | Array of result rows (each row is an array); omitted if adaptive timeout reached |
| `returnedRows` | Number of rows returned (`0` if adaptive timeout reached)                        |

metadata.breadcrumb: Submit SQL Query > Response Body — ADAPTIVE Mode

document:

These examples show ASYNC and ADAPTIVE requests and responses.

# Submit SQL Query > Apache Arrow Responses

Set `Accept: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` to request a binary Arrow IPC stream instead of JSON. Use an Arrow-compatible client library (such as [PyArrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/python/) or the [Apache Arrow Java library](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/java/)) to read the stream.

metadata.breadcrumb: Submit SQL Query > Apache Arrow Responses

document:
# Submit SQL Query > ASYNC Mode (Apache Arrow)

In ASYNC mode, the response body always contains only schema metadata with no data rows, regardless of the `Accept` header. Retrieve the `queryId` from the `x-hyperdb-status` response header and poll `GET /api/v3/query/{queryId}` for completion, then use `GET /api/v3/query/{queryId}/rows` or `/chunks/{chunkId}` with `Accept: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` to retrieve results.

metadata.breadcrumb: Submit SQL Query > ASYNC Mode (Apache Arrow)

document:
# Submit SQL Query > ADAPTIVE Mode (Apache Arrow)

Set `Accept: application/vnd.apache.arrow.stream` to receive an inline ADAPTIVE result as a binary Arrow IPC stream. If the query exceeds the adaptive timeout and falls back to ASYNC mode, the response body contains only schema metadata with no data rows. Retrieve the `queryId` from the `x-hyperdb-status` response header and poll `GET /api/v3/query/{queryId}` for completion.

# Submit SQL Query > Error Handling

V3 returns structured error objects with HTTP status codes.

| Status | Meaning                           |
| ------ | --------------------------------- |
| 400    | Invalid SQL or request payload    |
| 401    | Missing or invalid authentication |
| 408    | Request timed out                 |
| 429    | Rate limit exceeded               |
| 500    | Internal server error             |

Error responses include a rich error model with SQLSTATE codes and human-readable detail.

```json
{
  "error": "42601",
  "message": "syntax error [TraceId:03d7d84a302b827ea8f0fe1d251f4eaf]",
  "details": {
    "customerDetail": "line 1, column 49: ...",
    "errorSource": "User",
    "position": {
      "errorBeginCharacterOffset": "48",
      "errorEndCharacterOffset": "53"
    }
  }
}
```

The `position` field is included for syntax errors. `errorSource` indicates whether the error originated from user input (`"User"`) or the system. See [Query Services Status Codes](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/data-cloud-query-api-reference/c360a-api-queryservices-statuscodes.md) for the full reference.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > `AI_CLASSIFY`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ❌ Tableau Hyper API

Analyzes text and classifies it into the best matching category from a list of categories you define. This function uses the classification model to categorize support cases, customer inquiries, product feedback, and other unstructured text.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Syntax

```sql
ai_classify(<input_text>, <input_categories>)
```

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Required

- `<input_text>`: The [text](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/string.md) to classify.
- `<input_categories>`: A text [array](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array.md) of categories with at least one unique value. An empty category list results in the `Input categories cannot be empty` validation error message.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Returns

After analyzing the `input_text`, returns the category with the highest confidence score from the `input_categories`.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Considerations

- **Input text length**: The function supports input text up to 512 tokens (approximately 400-500 words). For longer text such as full emails or lengthy documents, split the content into shorter passages before classifying.
- **Best for short text**: This function works best on short, intent-rich text such as support case descriptions, product inquiries, and customer feedback.
- **Category consistency**: The `input_categories` parameter must be constant across all rows in the query.
- **Performance**: Requests to the function time out after 30 seconds.
- **First execution**: When executing this function on a large number of rows for the first time, you can encounter timeout or capacity errors. Start with smaller row counts and gradually increase volume to avoid these issues.
- **Non-NULL values**: `input_text` must be a non-NULL value. Add `IS NOT NULL` to the `WHERE` clause in your SQL statement to avoid `NULL` value errors.
- **Multilingual support**: The underlying model supports multiple languages.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Basic Usage

Classify issues in an automobile repair center based on the type of issue.

```sql
SELECT
  "issuesIdentified__c",
  ai_classify(input_text=>"issuesIdentified__c",
  input_categories=>'["Engine", "Chassis", "Electrical"]') AS category
  FROM "AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll"
```

Returns:

| issuesIdentified__c                                                               | category   |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- |
| Electrical system failure causing intermittent starting and dashboard warnings    | Electrical |
| Shock absorber replacement due to oil leakage and poor ride quality               | Chassis    |
| Engine overheating issue traced to failed radiator and thermostat replacement     | Engine     |
| Exhaust system repair and catalytic converter replacement                         | Engine     |
| Steering system malfunction requiring tie rod and power steering pump replacement | Chassis    |

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Filter Classification Results

Returns only the rows matching the defined classification.

```sql
WITH ClassifiedIssues AS (
  SELECT
    "serviceCenterName__c",
    "costOfService__c",
    "issuesIdentified__c",
    ai_classify(
      input_text => "issuesIdentified__c",
      input_categories => '["Engine", "Chassis", "Electrical"]'
    ) AS category
  FROM "AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll"
)
SELECT * FROM ClassifiedIssues
WHERE category = 'Engine';
```

Returns all reported vehicle issues related to the engine.

# `AI_CLASSIFY` > Related Documentation

- [Topic Classification](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360\_a_ai_predictive_model_classify.htm\&type=5): Learn about topic classification models, use cases, and integration options.

# Aggregate Functions > Aggregate Functions

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Functions that compute a single result from a set of input values. Use aggregate functions to:

- **Summarize data** by computing counts, sums, and averages.
- **Analyze distributions** with statistical functions such as standard deviation and variance.
- **Find extremes** with MIN and MAX values.
- **Compute percentiles** and identify modes in datasets.
- **Collect values** into an array, a delimited string, or a JSON array.

# Aggregate Functions > Considerations

- **Null handling**: Except for `COUNT`, `ARRAY_AGG` and `JSON_ARRAYAGG`, aggregate functions return NULL when no rows match. Use `coalesce(aggregate_func(...), default_value)` to substitute a default value.
- **Group by requirement**: Non-aggregated fields in the `SELECT` clause must appear in the `GROUP BY` clause.
- **Filter clause**: Use the [FILTER clause](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/filter-clause.md) to apply conditions to individual aggregates.

# Aggregate Functions > General-Purpose Aggregates

Common aggregate functions for summarizing data:

- [ANY_VALUE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/any-value.md) - Return an arbitrary value from the group.
- [APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/approx-count-distinct.md) - Compute an approximate count of distinct values.
- [AVG](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/avg.md) - Calculate the arithmetic mean.
- [BIT_AND](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/bit-and.md) - Compute bitwise AND of all values.
- [BIT_OR](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/bit-or.md) - Compute bitwise OR of all values.
- [BOOL_AND](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/bool-and.md) - Return `true` if all values are true.
- [BOOL_OR](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/bool-or.md) - Return `true` if any value is true.
- [COUNT](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/count.md) - Count rows or non-null values.
- [EVERY](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/every.md) - Return `true` if all values are true (alias for BOOL_AND).
- [MAX](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/max.md) - Find the maximum value.
- [MAX_BY](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/max-by.md) - Return the value from the row with the maximum key.
- [MIN](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/min.md) - Find the minimum value.
- [MIN_BY](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/min-by.md) - Return the value from the row with the minimum key.
- [SUM](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/sum.md) - Calculate the total.

# Aggregate Functions > Statistical Aggregates

Functions for statistical analysis:

- [CORR](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/corr.md) - Compute correlation coefficient.
- [COVAR_POP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/covar-pop.md) - Compute population covariance.
- [COVAR_SAMP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/covar-samp.md) - Compute sample covariance.
- [KURTOSIS](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/kurtosis.md) - Compute unbiased excess kurtosis.
- [SKEWNESS_POP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/skewness-pop.md) - Compute population skewness.
- [SKEWNESS_SAMP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/skewness-samp.md) - Compute sample skewness.
- [STDDEV/STDDEV_SAMP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/stddev.md) - Compute sample standard deviation.
- [STDDEV_POP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/stddev-pop.md) - Compute population standard deviation.
- [VAR_POP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/var-pop.md) - Compute population variance.
- [VARIANCE/VAR_SAMP](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/variance.md) - Compute sample variance.

:::tip
Cast the input of an aggregate function to force a different output type. For example, use `var_pop(CAST(A AS DOUBLE PRECISION))` to get a `double precision` result.
:::

# Aggregate Functions > Collection Aggregates

Functions that combine values from a group into a single array, string, or JSON array:

- [ARRAY_AGG](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array-agg.md) - Collect values into an array, with optional ordering and NULL handling.
- [JSON_ARRAYAGG](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/json-arrayagg.md) - Collect values into a JSON array, with optional ordering and NULL handling.
- [LISTAGG](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/listagg.md) - Concatenate values into a single delimited string.

# Aggregate Functions > Ordered-Set Aggregates

Aggregate functions that use the `WITHIN GROUP` syntax:

- [FIRST_VALUE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/first-value-ordered-set.md) - Return the `<value>` from the first row within each `GROUP BY` group after ordering by specified keys.
- [MODE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/mode.md) - Return the most frequent value.
- [PERCENTILE_CONT](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/percentile-cont.md) - Compute continuous percentile with interpolation.
- [PERCENTILE_DISC](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/percentile-disc.md) - Compute discrete percentile without interpolation.

For `MODE`, `PERCENTILE_CONT`, and `PERCENTILE_DISC`, NULL values in the sorted input are ignored where noted on each function page. Percentile functions require a fraction between 0 and 1. `FIRST_VALUE` does not use a fraction. Ordering follows the `ORDER BY` keys and `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST` modifiers.

# Aggregate Functions > Special Functions and Clauses

- [GROUPING](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/grouping.md) - Identify which columns are aggregated in grouping sets.
- [FILTER Clause](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/filter-clause.md) - Filter rows passed to aggregate functions.

# Aggregate Functions > Basic Aggregation

Calculate summary statistics.

```sql
SELECT
    count(*) AS total_orders,
    sum(amount) AS total_revenue,
    avg(amount) AS avg_order_value,
    min(amount) AS min_order,
    max(amount) AS max_order
FROM orders;
```

# Aggregate Functions > Aggregation with GROUP BY

Summarize data by category.

```sql
SELECT
    category,
    count(*) AS product_count,
    avg(price) AS avg_price
FROM products
GROUP BY category;
```

# Aggregate Functions > Using FILTER Clause

Compute multiple filtered aggregates in one query.

```sql
SELECT
    count(*) AS total,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'completed') AS completed,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending
FROM orders;
```

# Aggregate Functions > Statistical Analysis

Compute standard deviation and variance.

```sql
SELECT
    stddev(score) AS score_stddev,
    variance(score) AS score_variance
FROM test_results;
```

# Aggregate Functions > Percentile Calculation

Find median and quartiles.

```sql
SELECT
    percentile_cont(0.25) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS q1,
    percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS median,
    percentile_cont(0.75) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) AS q3
FROM employees;
```

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > `AI_SENTIMENT`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ❌ Tableau Hyper API

Performs sentiment analysis on text input and returns a sentiment label. This function uses a multilingual sentiment model to analyze customer feedback, support tickets, survey responses, and other unstructured text.

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > Required

- `input_text`: The [text](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/string.md) to analyze for sentiment. The function processes empty input values normally. The text must be a non-NULL value.

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > Returns

Returns a [text](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/string.md) sentiment label. Sentiment labels are:

- `Positive`: Text expressing positive sentiment
- `Negative`: Text expressing negative sentiment
- `Neutral`: Text expressing neutral sentiment
- `Mixed`: Text containing conflicting positive and negative signals
- `Unknown`: Text with unclear or indeterminate sentiment

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > Considerations

- **Input text length**: The function supports input text up to 512 tokens (approximately 400-500 words). For longer text such as full call transcripts or lengthy emails, split the content into shorter passages before analyzing.
- **Best for short text**: This function works best on short, intent-rich text such as support tickets, CRM notes, social media posts, and chat messages.
- **Performance**: Requests to the function time out after 30 seconds.
- **First execution**: When executing this function on a large number of rows for the first time, you can encounter timeout or capacity errors. Start with smaller row counts and gradually increase volume to avoid these issues.
- **Non-NULL values**: `input_text` must be a non-NULL value. Add `IS NOT NULL` to the `WHERE` clause in your SQL statement to avoid `NULL` value errors.
- **Multilingual support**: The underlying model supports multiple languages.

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > Using Table Data

Analyzes sentiment for multiple rows from a table.

```sql
SELECT
  "customerServiceFeedback__c",
  ai_sentiment("customerServiceFeedback__c") AS sentiment
FROM "AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll"
```

Returns the sentiment of the feedback for each row in the `AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll`.

# `AI_SENTIMENT` > Filtering Results

Show only positive feedback in a table.

```sql
WITH AnalyzedFeedback AS (
  SELECT
    "customerServiceFeedback__c",
    ai_sentiment("customerServiceFeedback__c") AS sentiment
  FROM "AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll"
)
SELECT * FROM AnalyzedFeedback
WHERE sentiment = 'positive';
```

Returns all positive feedback.

- [Sentiment Analysis](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360\_a_ai_predictive_model_sentiment.htm\&type=5): Learn about sentiment analysis models, use cases, and integration options.
- [AI Models in Data Cloud](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=data.c360\_a_ai_create_connect_activate_models.htm\&type=5): Read an overview of AI model capabilities.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta)

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ❌ Tableau Hyper API

:::note
`AI_GENERATE_TEXT` is a pilot or beta service that is subject to the Beta Services Terms at [Agreements - Salesforce.com](https://www.salesforce.com/company/legal/) or a written Unified Pilot Agreement if executed by Customer, and applicable terms in the [Product Terms Directory](https://ptd.salesforce.com/). Use of this pilot or beta service is at the Customer's sole discretion.
:::

Calls the Nemotron 3 Nano 30B (Beta) large language model (LLM) in a Data 360 SQL query to generate or summarize text. The function returns generated text for each row of data. To get started with this function in beta, turn on **Beta Generative AI Models**. To find this beta feature: under **Platform Tools** in **Setup**, go to **Einstein**, then to **Einstein Generative AI**, and then to **Einstein Setup**.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Syntax

```sql
ai_generate_text(<input_prompt>)
```

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Required

- `input_prompt`: The [text](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/string.md) prompt sent to the model. This can be a column, a literal, or an expression that composes a prompt from other columns (for example, by using the [string concatenation operator](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/concatenation-operator.md)).

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Returns

Returns generated [text](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/string.md) for each row according to the input prompt. A language model generates the output, so the same prompt can produce different text on different runs.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Considerations

- This is a beta function, and its output behavior may change during the beta period.
- When you turn on Beta Generative AI Models, the underlying model (NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 30B on Amazon (Beta)) is enabled by default. If the model isn't available, queries that call this function fail with a "model not available" error. To verify that the model is available, open the **App Launcher**, select **AI Models**, choose **Library (Generative)**, and confirm that NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 30B on Amazon (Beta) appears under **Model Name**. For the models that support generative AI features, see [Supported Models for Generative AI Features](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=ai.generative_ai_large_language_model_support.htm\&type=5).
- Requests to the function time out after 30 seconds. To stay within the timeout, reduce the amount of data the query processes. For example, use `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT` to cap the number of rows sent to the model.
- `input_prompt` must be a non-NULL value. Add `NON_NULL` to the `WHERE` clause in your SQL statement to avoid `NULL` value errors.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Generate Text from a Literal Prompt

Generate text from a single prompt.

```sql
SELECT ai_generate_text(input_prompt => 'Write a one-sentence thank-you note to a customer.') AS generated_text
```

Returns the generated text for the prompt.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Summarize Table Data

Generate a short summary of customer feedback for each row in a table.

```sql
SELECT
  "customerServiceFeedback__c",
  ai_generate_text('Summarize this customer feedback in one sentence: ' || "customerServiceFeedback__c") AS summary
FROM "AutomobileServiceFeedback__dll"
ORDER BY "date__c"
DESC LIMIT 10
```

This example builds the prompt for each row with the [string concatenation operator](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/concatenation-operator.md) (`||`). The operator joins the fixed instruction text, `'Summarize this customer feedback in one sentence: '`, to the value in the `customerServiceFeedback__c` column, so each row sends its own feedback text to the model as part of the prompt.

Returns a one-sentence summary of the feedback for each row.

# `AI_GENERATE_TEXT` (Beta) > Create a Unified Customer Profile Brief

Compose a prompt from identity, purchase, and service fields on a unified profile to generate a short brief for sales or service users.

```sql
SELECT
  "Id__c",
  ai_generate_text(
    'Write a two-sentence customer brief from these details. Name: ' || "FirstName__c" || ' ' || "LastName__c" ||
    '. Loyalty tier: ' || "LoyaltyTier__c" ||
    '. Last purchase category: ' || "LastPurchaseCategory__c" ||
    '. Recent service issue: ' || "LastCaseSummary__c"
  ) AS profile_brief
FROM "UnifiedIndividual__dlm"
ORDER BY "LastActivityDate__c" DESC
LIMIT 25
```

This example uses the [string concatenation operator](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/concatenation-operator.md) (`||`) to build a prompt from several profile fields, so the model generates a personalized brief for each customer. `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT` keeps the query within the 30-second timeout by capping how many rows are sent to the model.

# ALTER TABLE > ALTER TABLE

**Applies to:** ❌ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Change the definition of a table.

# ALTER TABLE > Description

`ALTER TABLE` changes the definition of an existing table. Hyper
currently only supports the following changes:

- `RENAME`

  - : The `RENAME` forms change the name of a table, the name of an
    individual column in a table, or the name of a constraint of the
    table. There is no effect on the stored data.

- `ADD COLUMN [ IF NOT EXISTS ]`

  - : This form adds a new column to the table, using the same syntax as
    [CREATE TABLE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/create-table.md). If `IF NOT EXISTS` is specified and a
    column already exists with this name, no error is thrown. In
    contrast to `CREATE TABLE`, which supports any variable-free
    expression, including non-constant expressions like random(), the
    default value here must be a constant.

- `DROP COLUMN [ IF EXISTS ]`

  - : This form drops a column from a table. Columns with indexes and
    table constraints can't be dropped.

- `ADD table_constraint [ NOT VALID ]`

  - : This form adds a new constraint to a table using the same syntax as
    [CREATE TABLE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/create-table.md).

Some forms of ALTER TABLE that act on a single table can be combined
into a list of multiple alterations to be applied together. It is
possible to add several columns and/or drop several columns in a single
command. It is also possible to create multiple column constraints in
a single command. It is not possible to combine altering columns with
adding constraints.

# ALTER TABLE > Parameters

- `IF EXISTS`

  - : Do not throw an error if the table does not exist.

- `<name>`

  - : The name (optionally schema-qualified) of an existing table to
    alter.

- `<column_name>`

  - : Name of a new or existing column.

- `<new_column_name>`

  - : New name for an existing column.

- `<new_name>`

  - : New name for the table.

- `<data_type>`

  - : Data type of the new column.

# ALTER TABLE > Notes

The key word `COLUMN` is noise and can be omitted.

Changing any part of a system catalog table is not permitted.

# ALTER TABLE > Examples

To add a column of type `text` to a table:

```sql
    ALTER TABLE distributors ADD COLUMN address text;
```

To drop a column from a table:

```sql
    ALTER TABLE distributors DROP COLUMN address;
```

To rename an existing column:

```sql
    ALTER TABLE distributors RENAME COLUMN address TO city;
```

To rename an existing table:

```sql
    ALTER TABLE distributors RENAME TO suppliers;
```

To add an unnamed assumed foreign key constraint to a table:

```sql
    ALTER TABLE distributors ADD ASSUMED FOREIGN KEY (address) REFERENCES addresses (address);
```

See [CREATE TABLE](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/create-table.md) for more examples of table constraints.

# `ANY_VALUE` > `ANY_VALUE`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Returns an arbitrary value from the set of input values. The result is non-deterministic.

# `ANY_VALUE` > Required

- `<expression>`: An expression of any type.

# `ANY_VALUE` > Returns

Returns a value of the same type as the input expression. Returns NULL if no rows are selected.

# `ANY_VALUE` > Considerations

- The value returned is implementation-defined and non-deterministic.
- Useful when you need any value from a group but don't care which one.
- Returns NULL when applied to an empty set.

# `ANY_VALUE` > Get Any Value from Group

Select an arbitrary value for each group.

```sql
SELECT department, any_value(employee_name) AS sample_employee
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;
```

Returns one employee name per department (which one is not guaranteed).

# `ANY_VALUE` > Related Documentation

- [Aggregate Functions](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/aggregate.md)
- [GROUP BY Clause](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/select-group-by.md)

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Computes an approximation of the count of distinct values with a specified expected relative error.

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Syntax

```sql
approx_count_distinct(<expression> [, <error>])
```

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Required

- `<expression>`: An expression of any type to count distinct values for.

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Optional

- `<error>`: A `double precision` value specifying the expected relative error. Must be in the range (0.002, 1]. Defaults to 0.023 (2.3% expected relative error).

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Returns

Returns a `bigint` representing the approximate count of distinct values.

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Considerations

- Faster than exact `count(distinct expression)` for large datasets.
- The error parameter controls the trade-off between accuracy and performance.
- Lower error values provide more accurate results but may require more computation.

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Approximate Distinct Count

Get an approximate count of distinct values.

```sql
SELECT approx_count_distinct(customer_id) AS approx_customers
FROM orders;
```

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > With Custom Error Rate

Specify a custom error rate for higher accuracy.

```sql
SELECT approx_count_distinct(product_id, 0.01) AS approx_products
FROM sales;
```

Returns an approximate count with 1% expected relative error.

# `APPROX_COUNT_DISTINCT` > Related Documentation

- [COUNT](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/count.md)
- [Aggregate Functions](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/aggregate.md)

# `ARRAY_AGG` > `ARRAY_AGG`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Collects the input values from a group into an array using an optional, user-supplied order.

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Syntax

```sql
array_agg([DISTINCT] <value> [ORDER BY <sort_expression> [ASC | DESC] [NULLS { FIRST | LAST }] [, ...]] [NULL ON NULL | ABSENT ON NULL])
```

Use with `GROUP BY` to build one array per group:

```sql
SELECT <group_columns>,
       array_agg(<value> ORDER BY <sort_expression>)
FROM <table>
GROUP BY <group_columns>;
```

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Required

- `<value>`: The expression collected into the array. Its result type becomes the element type of the returned array.

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Optional

- `DISTINCT`: Keeps only distinct values. When you use `DISTINCT`, the `ORDER BY` expression (including its collation) must match `<value>`.
- `ORDER BY <sort_expression> [, ...]`: Orders the elements within the array (an aggregate-local ordering). Each sort key accepts `ASC` / `DESC` and `NULLS FIRST` / `NULLS LAST`.
- `NULL ON NULL`: Collects `NULL` inputs as `NULL` array elements. This is the default.
- `ABSENT ON NULL`: Skips `NULL` inputs so they don't appear in the array.

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Returns

An array whose element type matches `<value>`.

**Null handling:**

- With the default `NULL ON NULL`, `NULL` inputs are kept as `NULL` array elements.
- With `ABSENT ON NULL`, `NULL` inputs are dropped. A group whose values are all `NULL` returns an empty array (`[]`).

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Considerations

- `array_agg` keeps `NULL`s by default (`NULL ON NULL`).
- The [`FILTER` clause](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/filter-clause.md) isn't supported for `array_agg`.
- When you combine `DISTINCT` with `ORDER BY`, the sort expression (and its collation) must match the aggregated value.
- If no `ORDER BY` is specified, the resulting array has an implementation-defined, non-deterministic order.
- `array_agg` with `ORDER BY` isn't supported in combination with `ROLLUP`, `CUBE`, or `GROUPING SETS`.
- To turn the resulting array into a delimited string, use [`ARRAY_TO_STRING`](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array-to-string.md). To expand an array back into rows, use [`UNNEST`](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/unnest.md).

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Aggregate values in a specified order, dropping NULLs

Order the elements by `timestamp` and skip `NULL` events.

```sql
SELECT array_agg(event ORDER BY timestamp ABSENT ON NULL)
FROM (VALUES ('completed', 2), (NULL, 3), ('started', 1)) AS events(event, timestamp);
```

Returns `["started","completed"]`.

# `ARRAY_AGG` > Keep NULLs (default behavior)

Without `ABSENT ON NULL`, `NULL` inputs are collected as `NULL` elements.

```sql
SELECT array_agg(v ORDER BY k)
FROM (VALUES (1, 1), (NULL, 2), (3, 3)) AS t(v, k);
```

Returns `[1,NULL,3]`.

# `ARRAY_AGG` > One array per group

Build a sorted array of product names for each category.

Inserts a value at the end of an array.

# `ARRAY_APPEND` > Syntax

```sql
array_append(<array>, <value>)
```

# `ARRAY_APPEND` > Required

- `<array>`: The array to append to.
- `<value>`: The value to insert at the end. The value must be NULL or match array element type, otherwise your SQL query will fail. Appending NULL changes the array element type to nullable.

# `ARRAY_APPEND` > Returns

Returns an array with the new value inserted at the end.

# `ARRAY_APPEND` > Append a Value

Add a value to the end of an array.


Returns `array[1, 2, 3, 4]`, with 4 added at the end.

# `ARRAY_APPEND` > Append NULL

Add a NULL value to the end of an array.

```sql
SELECT array_append(array[1, 2, 3], null) AS result;
```

Returns `array[1, 2, 3, null]`. Appending NULL to an array with a non-nullable element type changes the resulting element type to nullable.

# Array Constructor > Array Constructor

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Creates an array from a comma-separated list of values.

# Array Constructor > Syntax

```sql
ARRAY[<element1>, <element2>, ..., <elementN>]
```

# Array Constructor > Required

- `<element1>, <element2>, ..., <elementN>`: Values to include in the array. All elements must be of compatible types that can be coerced to a common element type.

# Array Constructor > Returns

Returns an `ARRAY` that contains the specified elements. Data 360 SQL automatically infers the array type from the provided elements.

# Array Constructor > Considerations

- All array elements must be of compatible types.
- Elements can be literals, column references, or expressions.
- Empty arrays can be created with `ARRAY[]`.
- Arrays can contain `NULL` values.
- Type coercion applies when elements are of different but compatible types.
- If no `null` values are in the constructor, Data 360 SQL infers the element type as `not null`.
- Arrays are limited to 4 GB in size
- Arrays cannot be nested (see [Array Type](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array.md#limitations)).

Create a simple array of numeric values.

# `ARRAY_CONTAINS` > `ARRAY_CONTAINS`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Checks whether a specified value is present in an array.

# `ARRAY_CONTAINS` > Returns

# `ARRAY_CONTAINS` > Considerations

# `ARRAY_CONTAINS` > Check for Existing Value

Check whether a value exists in an array.

```sql
SELECT array_contains(array[1, 3, 4], 3) AS contains_three;
```

# `ARRAY_CONTAINS` > Check for Missing Value

Check whether a value is present in an array.

```sql
SELECT array_contains(array[1, 3, 4], 2) AS contains_two;
```

Returns `false` because 2 isn't present in the array.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > `ARRAY_FILTER`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Returns a new array containing only the elements for which the provided lambda expression returns true.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Syntax

```sql
array_filter(<array>, <lambda>)
```

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Required

- `<array>`: The input array to filter.
- `<lambda>`: A lambda expression that takes one parameter and returns a boolean value. Elements for which the lambda returns true are included in the result.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Returns

Returns an array containing only the elements where the lambda expression evaluated to true. Returns NULL if the input array is NULL. Returns an empty array if no elements match the condition.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Considerations

- The lambda expression must return a boolean value. Non-boolean return types result in an error.
- The lambda can't reference columns or variables from the outer query scope.
- The order of elements in the result matches their order in the input array.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Filter Even Numbers

Keep only even numbers from an array.

```sql
SELECT array_filter(ARRAY[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], lambda x: x % 2 = 0) AS evens;
```

Returns `[2, 4, 6]`.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Filter with String Pattern Matching

Keep strings that don't contain uppercase letters.

```sql
SELECT array_filter(
  ARRAY['abc', 'very long string', 'UPPER case', 'lower case'],
  lambda x: NOT regexp_like(x, '[A-Z]')
) AS lowercase_only;
```

Returns `["abc", "very long string", "lower case"]`.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Filter Multidimensional Arrays

Filter nested arrays based on their contents.

```sql
SELECT array_filter(
  ARRAY[ARRAY[1, 2, 3], ARRAY[4, 5, 6], ARRAY[2, 3, 4]],
  lambda x: array_contains(x, 3)
) AS contains_three;
```

Returns `[[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4]]`.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Filter with Comparison

Keep elements greater than a threshold.

```sql
SELECT array_filter(ARRAY[10, 25, 5, 30, 15], lambda x: x > 20) AS large_values;
```

Returns `[25, 30]`.

# `ARRAY_FILTER` > Combine with Other Array Functions

Chain ARRAY_FILTER with other array operations.

```sql
SELECT array_length(
  array_filter(ARRAY[1, 2, 3, 4, 5], lambda x: x > 2)
) AS count_above_two;
```

Returns `3`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based)

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Generate an array of time-based values, from `start` to `stop` with a given `step` size.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Syntax

```sql
array_generate_series(<start>, <stop>, <step>)
```

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Required

- `<start>`: The start value of the series. Can be of type `DATE`, `TIMESTAMP`, or `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE`.
- `<stop>`: The end value of the series. Must be of the same type as `<start>`.
- `<step>`: The step size as an `INTERVAL`. Unlike the numerical version of `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES`, the step size is always required for time-based series.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Returns

Returns an `ARRAY` containing the generated series of values.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Considerations

This function is equivalent to the [generate_series (Time-based)](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/generate-series-time.md) function, with the only difference that it returns an array instead of a set of rows.
Read the documentation on `generate_series (Time-based)` for more details.
All considerations also apply to `array_generate_series` with the following differences:

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Basic Usage with Dates

Generate an array of months between two dates.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series('2017-01-01'::date, '2017-03-01'::date, '1 month'::interval);
```

returns `["2017-01-01","2017-02-01","2017-03-01"]`

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Usage with Timestamps

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series('2017-01-01 01:02:03'::timestamp, '2017-03-01 01:02:03'::timestamp, '1 month'::interval);
```

returns `["2017-01-01 01:02:03","2017-02-01 01:02:03","2017-03-01 01:02:03"]`

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Additional Examples

Take a look at the [generate_series examples](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/generate-series-time.md#examples) for additional examples.
They also apply to `array_generate_series`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Time-based) > Related Documentation

- [Array Functions](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/arrays.md)
- [`ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical)](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array-generate-series.md) - the numerical version of this function
- [`generate_series` (Time-based)](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/generate-series-time.md) - the set-returning version of this function

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical)

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Creates an array of sequential values within a range.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Syntax

```sql
array_generate_series(<start>, <stop>[, <step>])
```

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Required

- `<start>`: The starting value of the sequence.
- `<stop>`: The ending value of the sequence (inclusive).

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Optional

- `<step>`: The increment between values. The default is 1.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Returns

Returns an array that contains sequential values from `start` to `stop`, incrementing by `step`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Considerations

- If you use a negative step, make sure `<start>` is greater than `<stop>`. If `<start>` is less than or equal to `<stop>`, the function returns an empty array.
- A negative step generates a descending sequence. A positive step generates an ascending sequence.
- This function is equivalent to the [generate_series (Numerical)](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/generate-series.md) function but returns an array instead of a set of rows.
- Both the `start` and `stop` values are included in the generated series.
- The step size must be non-zero.
- The step size can also be negative. For negative step sizes, `start` must be greater than `stop`.
- For positive step sizes, if `start` is greater than `stop`, the function returns no rows.
- For negative step sizes, if `start` is less than `stop`, the function returns no rows.
- If any input is `null`, the function returns no rows.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Basic Usage

Create an array of integers from 1 to 5.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series(1, 5) AS result;
```

Returns `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Generate Sequence with Step

Create an array of integers from 1 to 5 with step 2.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series(1, 5, 2) AS result;
```

Returns `[1, 3, 5]`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Reverse Sequence with Negative Step

Create an array counting down from 5 to 1 in increments of 2.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series(5, 1, -2) AS result;
```

Returns `[5, 3, 1]`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Decimal Reverse Sequence

Create a descending array with decimal values.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series(3.7, 3.0, -0.3) AS result;
```

Returns `[3.7, 3.4, 3.1]`.

# `ARRAY_GENERATE_SERIES` (Numerical) > Negative Step with Increasing Range (Empty Result)

When the step direction doesn't match the range direction, an empty array is returned.

```sql
SELECT array_generate_series(1, 5, -1) AS result;
```

Returns `[]`.

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > `ARRAY_PREPEND`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Inserts a value at the start of an array.

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Syntax

```sql
array_prepend(<value>, <array>)
```

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Required

- `<value>`: The value to insert at the start of the array. The value must match the array element type.
- `<array>`: The array to prepend to.

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Returns

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Considerations

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Prepend a Value


Returns `array[1, 2, 3, 4]`, with 1 inserted at the beginning.

# `ARRAY_PREPEND` > Prepend NULL

Add a NULL value to the front of an array.

```sql
SELECT array_prepend(null, array[2, 3, 4]) AS result;
```


- `ascending`: A boolean flag that indicates the sort order. When `true` (default), sorts in ascending order. When `false`, sorts in descending order.

# `ARRAY_SORT` > Returns

Returns an array with elements sorted in the specified order. NULL values are always first in the output array.

# `ARRAY_SORT` > Considerations

- NULL values are always first in the output array, regardless of sort order.
- The default sort order is ascending.

# `ARRAY_SORT` > Sort in Ascending Order

Sort an array in ascending order (default behavior).

```sql
SELECT array_sort(array[3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]) AS result;
```

```sql
SELECT array_sort(array[3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6], false) AS result;
```

Sort an array that contains NULL values.

```sql
SELECT array_sort(array[3, null, 1, null, 2]) AS result;
```

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > `ARRAY_TO_STRING`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Converts an array to a string using a separator and an optional null indicator.

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Syntax

```sql
array_to_string(<array>, <separator>[, null_string])
```

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Required

- `<array>`: The array to convert.
- `<separator>`: The delimiter to insert between elements.

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Optional

- `null_string`: The string to use for NULL elements.

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Returns

Returns a text value that contains all array elements joined by the separator. Without the optional `null_string` parameter, NULL elements are omitted from the output.

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Basic Conversion

Convert an array to a semicolon-separated string.

```sql
SELECT array_to_string(array[1, 2, 3, NULL], ';') AS result;
```

Returns `'1;2;3'`, joining all elements with semicolons. The `NULL` element was ignored because no `NULL` value was specified.

# `ARRAY_TO_STRING` > Handle NULL Elements

Convert an array with NULL values using a custom null indicator.


# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > `ARRAY_TRANSFORM`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Applies a lambda expression to each element (or corresponding elements from multiple arrays) and returns a new array with the transformed values.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Syntax

```sql
array_transform(<array1>[, <array2>, ...], <lambda>)
```

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Required

- `<array1>`: The first input array.
- `<lambda>`: A lambda expression that defines the transformation. The number of parameters in the lambda must match the number of input arrays.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Optional

- `<array2>, ...`: Additional input arrays. When multiple arrays are provided, the lambda receives corresponding elements from each array. All arrays must have the same length.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Returns

Returns an array with the same length as the input arrays, where each element is the result of applying the lambda expression to the corresponding input element(s). Returns NULL if any input array is NULL.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Considerations

- All input arrays must have the same length. Mismatched lengths result in an error.
- NULL elements in the input arrays propagate through the lambda. If any input element is NULL, the corresponding output element is typically NULL (depending on the lambda expression).
- The lambda's return type determines the output array's element type. If the lambda returns only NULL, you must explicitly cast it to a specific type.
- Empty arrays return an empty array.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Transform a Single Array

Double each element in an array.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(ARRAY[1, 2, 3], lambda x: x * 2) AS doubled;
```

Returns `[2, 4, 6]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Combine Two Arrays

Add corresponding elements from two arrays.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(ARRAY[1, 2, 3], ARRAY[10, 20, 30], lambda x, y: x + y) AS sums;
```

Returns `[11, 22, 33]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > String Concatenation

Concatenate corresponding strings from two arrays.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(
  ARRAY['hello', 'good'],
  ARRAY[' world', ' bye'],
  lambda x, y: x || y
) AS greetings;
```

Returns `["hello world", "good bye"]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Conditional Transformation

Use CASE to apply conditional logic.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(
  ARRAY[1, 5, 3],
  ARRAY[4, 2, 6],
  lambda x, y: CASE WHEN x > y THEN x ELSE y END
) AS maximums;
```

Returns `[4, 5, 6]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Comparison Operations

Compare corresponding elements and return boolean results.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(ARRAY[1, 5, 3], ARRAY[4, 2, 6], lambda x, y: x > y) AS comparisons;
```

Returns `[false, true, false]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Three or More Arrays

Combine elements from three arrays.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(
  ARRAY[1, 2],
  ARRAY[3, 4],
  ARRAY[5, 6],
  lambda x, y, z: x + y + z
) AS totals;
```

Returns `[9, 12]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > NULL Handling

NULL elements propagate through the transformation.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(ARRAY[1, NULL, 3], ARRAY[4, 5, 6], lambda x, y: x + y) AS result;
```

Returns `[5, NULL, 9]`.

# `ARRAY_TRANSFORM` > Nested Array Transform

Use nested calls to chain transformations.

```sql
SELECT array_transform(
  array_transform(ARRAY[1, 2], ARRAY[3, 4], lambda x, y: x + y),
  ARRAY[10, 20],
  lambda x, y: x * y
) AS result;
```

Returns `[40, 120]`.

# Array Type > Array Type

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

An array is a sequential collection of elements in a single SQL value. Arrays can model dependent information with an inherent ordering in a single row. For example, time series data from longitudinal studies or embedding vectors from machine learning models.

Array type syntax:

```sql
array(<atomic type> [not null])
```

The optional `not null` specifier indicates if array elements can be `null`. For example, `array(integer not null)` represents a range of non-null integer elements.

All array types have these properties.

- Arrays have variable length. Within a column, arrays aren’t required to have the same number of elements.
- Arrays are one-dimensional.

For a comprehensive overview of supported operations on arrays, see [Array Functions](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/arrays.md).

# Array Type > Creating Arrays

You can create arrays in two ways.

- By using the [Array Constructor](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/array-constructor.md) syntax.

- By casting a string literal to an array with `::array(<type>)`.

```sql
select '[1,2,3]'::array(integer);

select '[one,two,three]'::array(text);
```

An array string literal consists of a comma-separated list of element literals surrounded by square brackets `[...]`. The element literal syntax is identical to that of the respective atomic type.

For string array types, any upper or lower case variant of the element literal `null` is parsed as a `null` value. To specify the string `"null"`, escape the element literal by using double quotes. For example:

```sql
select '[null, "null"]'::array(text)
```

Returns: `[NULL,"null"]` — a null element, followed by the string `'null'`.

When returning an array of text types, every non-null element is quoted.

See [Type Conversions](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/type-conversion.md) for `CAST`, `TRY_CAST`, and `::`.

# Array Type > Element Types and Nullability (Part 1)

Arrays are strongly typed and use the array’s element type for all elements in the array. The element type is a defining part of the array’s overall type, meaning that `array(integer)` is a different type than `array(boolean)` or `array(text)`. You can build an array from any [atomic type](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/datatypes.md#atomic-types) supported by Data 360 SQL.

Part of an array’s element type is the element’s nullability. For example, `array(smallint)` is different from `array(smallint not null)`.

These four options represent different array types.

| Type                               | Array nullable? | Elements nullable? | Possible values                     |
| :--------------------------------- | :-------------- | :----------------- | :---------------------------------- |
| `array(integer)`                   | yes             | yes                | `[]`,`[1,2,3]`,`[1,2,null]`, `null` |
| `array(integer not null)`          | yes             | no                 | `[]`,`[1,2,3]`,`null`               |
| `array(integer) not null`          | no              | yes                | `[]`,`[1,2,3]`,`[1,2,null]`         |
| `array(integer not null) not null` | no              | no                 | `[]`,`[1,2,3]`                      |

metadata.breadcrumb: Array Type > Element Types and Nullability (Part 1)

document:
# Array Type > Element Types and Nullability (Part 2)

The inner nullability of an array type can be changed by casting, using the conventional [cast syntax](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/type-conversion.md).

Nullable to non-nullable:

```sql
select ('[1,2,3]'::array(integer))::array(integer not null)
```

Non-nullable to nullable:

```sql
select ('[1,2,3]'::array(integer not null))::array(integer)
```

A cast from a non-nullable element type to its nullable counterpart always succeeds. The reverse direction succeeds if the array doesn’t contain `null` elements. Casts across element types aren’t supported. The only exception is casts from array to string types.

:::info
Non-nullable element types use less memory and turn on optimizations for certain array operations. Use the most “restrictive” element type possible based on the use case at hand.
:::

# Array Type > Limitations

Arrays have these limitations.

- The size of an array is limited to 4GB.
- Arrays can’t be nested.
- Arrays can’t be used as column types in non-temporary tables.

:::note
See the restrictions regarding array support in [external formats](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/external-formats.md).
:::

# `BINARY_QUANTIZE` > `BINARY_QUANTIZE`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Encodes each array element into a single bit, compressing the vector by approximately 32x.

# `BINARY_QUANTIZE` > Required

# Binary Data Type > Binary Data Type

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

The `bytes` data type allows the storage of binary strings.

A binary string is a sequence of octets (or bytes). Binary strings differ from character strings in two ways.

- Binary strings can store octets of value zero and other non-printable octets.
- Operations on binary strings process the actual bytes. Processing of character strings depends on locale settings.

Use binary strings to store raw byte data and use character strings to store text.

Data 360 SQL provides these aliases for the `bytes` type.

- `bytea`
- `blob`
- `varbinary`

The input format is different from `bytes`, but the provided functions and operators are mostly the same.

# Binary Data Type > Bytes Hex Format

The `bytes` type supports input and output by using the hex format.

The hex format encodes binary data as two hexadecimal digits per byte, the most significant nibble first. The sequence `\x` precedes the string. To escape the backslash character, use `\\x`. For input, the hexadecimal digits can be either upper or lower case.

Example:

```sql
    SELECT '\xDEADBEEF'::bytea;
```

# Boolean Type > Boolean Type

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

The `boolean` type can have three states: true, false, and unknown. The SQL `NULL` value represents unknown. You can represent boolean constants in SQL queries with the SQL key words `TRUE`, `FALSE`, and `NULL`.

A [comparison](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/comparison.md) or a similar function call can result in a boolean value. You can also use [logical operators](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/logical.md) to combine boolean values.

To parse a `boolean` from a string, use one of these strings.

| True   | False   |
| :----- | :------ |
| `true` | `false` |
| `yes`  | `no`    |
| `on`   | `off`   |
| `1`    | `0`     |
| `t`    | `f`     |
| `y`    | `n`     |

Data 360 SQL ignores leading or trailing whitespace and isn’t case-sensitive. To use the string representations, provide the generic string-literal constant syntax. For example, 'yes'::boolean.

Data 360 SQL can’t automatically infer the type of `NULL` literals. To prevent errors, explicitly cast `NULL` to `boolean`. For example, `NULL::boolean`.

Converting a `boolean` to a string always emits either `true` or `false`, as shown in this example.

The table `test1` is defined as:

| a     | b       |
| ----- | ------- |
| true  | sic est |
| false | non est |

Column `a` is a boolean value and column `b` is a text value.

```sql
SELECT * FROM test1;
```

Results:

| a     | b       |
| ----- | ------- |
| true  | sic est |
| false | non est |

```sql
SELECT * FROM test1 WHERE a;

```

Results:

| a    | b       |
| ---- | ------- |
| true | sic est |

# Comparison Operators > Comparison Operators

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Comparison operators compare a value against another value. Comparison operators are binary operators that return values of type `boolean`.

| Operator     | Description              |
| :----------- | :----------------------- |
| `<`          | less than                |
| `>`          | greater than             |
| `<=`         | less than or equal to    |
| `>=`         | greater than or equal to |
| `=`          | equal                    |
| `<>` or `!=` | not equal                |

# Comparison Operators > `BETWEEN`

The `BETWEEN` predicate simplifies range tests.

```sql
<a> BETWEEN <x> AND <y>
<a> NOT BETWEEN <x> AND <y>
```

`a BETWEEN x AND y` is equivalent to `a >= x AND a <= y`. `BETWEEN` treats the endpoint values as included in the range. `NOT BETWEEN` does the opposite comparison: `a NOT BETWEEN x AND y` is equivalent to `a < x OR a > y`.

While the normal comparison operators and `BETWEEN` ignore NULLs.

# Comparison Operators > `NULL` Expressions (Part 1)

These comparison functions are available in Data 360 SQL.

```sql
<a> IS DISTINCT FROM <b>
<a> IS NOT DISTINCT FROM <b>
<expression> IS NULL
<expression> IS NOT NULL
<expression> ISNULL -- nonstandard syntax
<expression> NOTNULL -- nonstandard syntax
<boolean_expression> IS TRUE
<boolean_expression> IS NOT TRUE -- is false or unknown
<boolean_expression> IS FALSE
<boolean_expression> IS NOT FALSE -- is true or unknown
<boolean_expression> IS UNKNOWN
<boolean_expression> IS NOT UNKNOWN -- is true or false
```

Ordinary comparison operators yield null (signifying "unknown") if either input is null. For example, `7 = NULL` returns null. If this behavior doesn't fit your use case, use the `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` predicates.

- `a IS DISTINCT FROM b`
- `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b`.

For non-null inputs, `IS DISTINCT FROM` is the same as the `<>` operator. However, if both inputs are null it returns false, and if one input is null it returns true. `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` is identical to `=` for non-null inputs, but returns true if both inputs are null, and false if one input is null. These predicates act as though null is a normal data value, rather than an unknown.

To check whether a value is or isn't null, use the predicates:

# Comparison Operators > `NULL` Expressions (Part 2)

If either input is null, ordinary comparison operators yield null, signifying “unknown”. For example, `7 = NULL` returns null. If this behavior doesn’t fit your use case, use the `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` predicates.

- `expression IS NOT NULL`
- `expression ISNULL`
- `expression NOTNULL`.

For non-null inputs, `IS DISTINCT FROM` is the same as the `<>` operator. However, if both inputs are null, it returns false. If one input is null, it returns true. `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` is identical to `=` for non-null inputs, but it returns true if both inputs are null and false if one input is null. These predicates act as though null is a normal data value rather than an unknown.

To check whether a value is or isn’t null, use the predicates.

- `IS NOT TRUE`
- `IS FALSE`
- `IS NOT FALSE`
- `IS UNKNOWN`
- `IS NOT UNKNOWN`.

You can also test boolean values by using the predicates.

# Comparison Operators > `IN` and `NOT IN`

`IN` and `NOT IN` compare an expression against multiple values. They use the syntax

```sql
<expression> IN ( <value>, ... )
<expression> NOT IN ( <value>, ... )
```

These tests always return true or false, even if the operand is null. A null input is treated as the logical value “unknown”. Notice that `IS UNKNOWN` and `IS NOT UNKNOWN` are effectively the same as `IS NULL` and `IS NOT NULL`, respectively, except that the input expression is of Boolean type.

The right-hand side is a parenthesized list of scalar expressions. The value from the left-hand side is compared against each of the expressions from the right-hand side.

`IN` and `NOT IN` compare an expression against multiple values. They use this syntax.

For `NOT IN` the result is true if the left-hand expression's result is unequal to all of the right-hand expressions. This is a shorthand notation for `expression <> value1 AND expression <> value2 AND ...`

If the left-hand expression returns null, or if there are no equal right-hand values and at least one right-hand expression returns null, the result of the `IN`/`NOT IN` construct is null.

`IN` and `NOT IN` are syntactically related to the [subquery forms](/docs/data/data-cloud-query-guide/references/dc-sql-reference/subquery-comparison.md#in) but don't involve subqueries.

# Conditional Expressions > Conditional Expressions

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

The conditional expressions select one of multiple result values.

# Conditional Expressions > `CASE` (Part 1)

The SQL CASE expression is a generic conditional expression, similar to if/else statements in other programming languages. CASE clauses can be used wherever an expression is valid CASE expressions have two variants.

```sql
CASE
    WHEN <condition> THEN <result>
    [WHEN ...]
    [ELSE <result>]
END

CASE <expression>
    WHEN <value> THEN <result>
    [WHEN ...]
    [ELSE <result>]
END
```

In the first variant, each `condition` is an expression that returns a boolean result. If the condition’s result is true, the value of the CASE expression is the `result` that follows the condition, and the rest of the CASE expression isn’t processed. If the condition’s result isn’t true, any subsequent WHEN clauses are examined in the same manner. If no WHEN `condition` yields true, the value of the CASE expression is the `result` of the ELSE clause. If the ELSE clause is omitted and no condition is true, the result is null.

For example, the query:

The table `test` is defined as:

```sql
a
--
1
2
3
```

```sql
SELECT a,
    CASE
        WHEN a=1 THEN 'one'
        WHEN a=2 THEN 'two'
        ELSE 'other'
    END
FROM test;
```

Returns the result:

```sql
a | case
--+-------
1 | one
2 | two
3 | other
```

The second form of CASE expressions, called a simple case expressions, is similar to a `switch` statement in C.

# Conditional Expressions > `CASE` (Part 2)

First, `expression` is computed and then compared to each of the `value` expressions in the WHEN clauses until one is found that is equal to it. If no match is found, the `result` of the ELSE clause (or a null value) is returned.

For example, the previous example can be written as a simple CASE expression.

```sql
SELECT a,
    CASE a
        WHEN 1 THEN 'one'
        WHEN 2 THEN 'two'
        ELSE 'other'
    END
FROM test;
```

A CASE expression doesn’t evaluate any subexpressions that aren’t required to determine the result. For example, this CASE expression is a potential way to avoid a division-by-zero failure.

```sql
SELECT ... WHERE CASE WHEN x <> 0 THEN y/x > 1.5 ELSE false END;
```

The data types of all the `result` expressions must be convertible to a single output type.

# Conditional Expressions > `COALESCE`

```sql
coalesce(<value>, ...)
```

The `COALESCE` function returns the first of its arguments that isn't null. Null is returned only if all arguments are null. It’s often used to substitute a default value for null values if data is retrieved for display, for example:

```sql
SELECT coalesce(description, short_description, '(none)') ...
```

This function returns `description` if it isn’t null. Or it returns `short_description` if it isn’t null. Otherwise, it returns `(none)`.

`COALESCE` only evaluates the arguments that are needed to determine the result. Arguments after the first non-null argument aren’t evaluated.

# Conditional Expressions > `NULLIF`

```sql
nullif(<value1>, <value2>)
```

The `NULLIF` function returns a null value if `value1` equals `value2`. Otherwise, it returns `value1`. This function can be used to perform the inverse operation of the previous `COALESCE` example.

```sql
SELECT nullif(value, '(none)')
```

In this example, if `value` is `(none)`, NULLIF returns null, otherwise the value of `value` is returned.

# Conditional Expressions > `GREATEST` and `LEAST`

```sql
greatest(value, ...)
least(value, ...)
greatest(PRESERVE NULLS value, ...)
least(PRESERVE NULLS value, ...)
```

The `GREATEST` and `LEAST` functions choose the largest or smallest value from a list of expressions. The expressions must all be convertible to a common data type, and is the type of the result.

By default, NULL values in the list are ignored. The result is NULL if all of the inputs evaluate to NULL. To preserve NULL inputs, use \`PRESERVE NULLS. In this case, the result is NULL if any input is NULL.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS`

**Applies to:** ✅ Data 360 SQL ✅ Tableau Hyper API

Checks whether a string contains a specified substring or character value. `CONTAINS` performs a case-sensitive search, while `ICONTAINS` performs a case-insensitive search.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Syntax

```sql
contains(<string>, <substring>)
icontains(<string>, <substring>)
```

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Required

- `<string>`: The string to search within.
- `<substring>`: The substring or character to search for.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Returns

Returns a boolean value indicating whether the string contains the substring, or NULL if either argument is NULL.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Considerations

- **Empty substring**: An empty substring returns `true` for any non-NULL string.
- **Literal matching**: Treats the `_` and `%` characters as literal characters, not wildcards.
- **Collation support**: Use collations for locale-aware matching, including case-insensitive (`_ci`) and accent-insensitive (`_ai`) options.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Case-Sensitive Search

Check whether a string contains a substring (case-sensitive).

```sql
SELECT contains('Hello World', 'World') AS result;
```

Returns `true`.

```sql
SELECT contains('Hello World', 'world') AS result;
```

Returns `false` because the case doesn’t match.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Case-Insensitive Search

Check whether a string contains a substring (case-insensitive).

```sql
SELECT icontains('Hello World', 'world') AS result;
```

Returns `true` because `icontains` ignores case differences.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > NULL Handling

Returns NULL when either argument is NULL.

```sql
SELECT contains('tableau', NULL) AS result;
```

Returns `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT contains(NULL, 'water') AS result;
```

Returns `NULL`.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Empty Substring

An empty substring is always contained in any string.

```sql
SELECT contains('tableau', '') AS result;
```

Returns `true`.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Literal Matching

Matches the `_` and `%` characters literally, not as wildcards.

```sql
SELECT contains('Tableau', '_') AS result;
```

Returns `false` because it treats `_` as a literal underscore.

```sql
SELECT contains('Tableau_', '_') AS result;
```

Returns `true`.

# `CONTAINS` / `ICONTAINS` > Using Collations

Use collations for locale-aware matching.

```sql
SELECT contains(name COLLATE "de_DE_ci", 'ABC') AS result
FROM products;
```

Performs a case-insensitive search using German locale rules.

```sql
SELECT contains(name COLLATE "en_US_ai", 'cafe') AS result
FROM products;
```

Performs an accent-insensitive search using the US English locale rules, matching both "cafe" and "café".
